title: First Law of Thermodynamics
short_intro: The first law of thermodynamics is a statement of the principle of conservation of energy applied to thermodynamic systems. It establishes that internal energy is a state function and links heat, work, and internal energy changes.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Sign convention for heat and work, cyclic processes, application to isothermal, isobaric, isochoric, and adiabatic processes, and fundamental definitions of internal energy.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Differential formulation dQ = dU + dW, molar heat capacities C_p and C_v relation (C_p - C_v = R), application to non-quasi-static processes, and microscopic link with the kinetic theory of gases.

prerequisites: Mechanical work and energy in mechanics

concept_notes.heading: Statement of the First Law
bullets: Energy can be neither created nor destroyed, only transformed from one form to another.

When a system undergoes a thermodynamic change from an initial state to a final state, the net heat supplied to the system minus the work done by the system depends only on the initial and final states.
Expressed mathematically as dQ = dU + dW, where dQ is heat added, dU is change in internal energy, and dW is work done by the system.

concept_notes.heading: Internal Energy as a State Function
bullets: Internal energy U is a macroscopic property representing the total microscopic kinetic and potential energy of the molecules in the system.
It is a state function, meaning its change depends solely on the initial and final equilibrium states, independent of the path taken.
For a complete cyclic process, the net change in internal energy is zero (delta U = 0).

concept_notes.heading: Sign Conventions
bullets: Heat (Q) added to the system is positive (+Q); heat lost by the system is negative (-Q).
Work (W) done by the system (expansion) is positive (+W); work done on the system (compression) is negative (-W).
Increase in internal energy (U) is positive (+dU); decrease is negative (-dU).

concept_notes.heading: Thermodynamic Processes
bullets: Isothermal process: Temperature is constant, leading to delta U = 0, hence Q = W.
Adiabatic process: No heat exchange (Q = 0), leading to delta U = -W (work done at the expense of internal energy).
Isochoric process: Volume is constant (dW = 0), leading to Q = delta U.

derivations.title: Relation between Molar Heat Capacities (C_p - C_v = R)
derivations.conditions: One mole of an ideal gas
steps: Apply the first law for a constant volume (isochoric) process: dQ_v = dU = C_v dT, since dW = P dV = 0.
Apply the first law for a constant pressure (isobaric) process: dQ_p = dU + P dV = C_p dT.
Substitute internal energy change dU = C_v dT into the isobaric equation: C_p dT = C_v dT + P dV.
For one mole of an ideal gas, the equation of state is PV = RT, differentiating gives P dV = R dT.
Substitute P dV = R dT into the energy balance equation: C_p dT = C_v dT + R dT.
Divide throughout by dT to yield the final relation.

derivations.title: Work Done in an Isothermal Reversible Expansion of an Ideal Gas
derivations.conditions: Quasi-static isothermal expansion of n moles of an ideal gas
steps: Start with the definition of work done: W = \int_{V_1}^{V_2} P \, dV.
Use the ideal gas equation of state to express pressure: P = \frac{nRT}{V}.
Substitute P into the work integral: W = \int_{V_1}^{V_2} \frac{nRT}{V} \, dV.
Since temperature T is constant during an isothermal process, factor out nRT: W = nRT \int_{V_1}^{V_2} \frac{1}{V} \, dV.
Integrate the logarithmic term: W = nRT \ln\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right).

graphs_and_experiments.title: P-V Diagram for Isothermal and Adiabatic Processes
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Two curves starting from the same initial state (P_1, V_1) on a P-V graph, showing the adiabatic curve steeper than the isothermal curve.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of the adiabatic curve is -\gamma P / V, whereas the slope of the isothermal curve is -P / V. Since \gamma > 1, the adiabatic curve is steeper.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently tested in multiple-choice questions comparing work done and final temperatures.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Cyclic Process on a P-V Diagram
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A closed loop (clockwise or counter-clockwise) on a P-V plane.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The net work done during a complete cycle equals the enclosed area of the loop. Clockwise represents net positive work (heat engine), counter-clockwise represents net negative work (heat pump/refrigerator).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to evaluate net heat absorbed and net work done in thermodynamic cycles.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Joule's Paddle-Wheel Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A schematic of a falling weight connected via a string and pulley to a paddle-wheel submerged in an insulated container of water.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrated the mechanical equivalence of heat. Work done by falling masses converted directly into thermal energy, increasing the temperature of water, establishing that work and heat are interchangeable forms of energy.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual questions on the equivalence of mechanical work and thermal energy.

solved_numericals.question: In a thermodynamic process, a system absorbs 500 J of heat and simultaneously does 200 J of work on its surroundings. What is the change in internal energy of the system?
solution_steps: Identify given values using sign convention: dQ = +500 J (heat absorbed), dW = +200 J (work done by system).
Write the first law of thermodynamics: dQ = dU + dW.
Rearrange to solve for change in internal energy: dU = dQ - dW.
Substitute values: dU = 500 J - 200 J = 300 J.

solved_numericals.question: Two moles of an ideal monoatomic gas (C_v = 3R/2) are heated at constant pressure from 27 °C to 127 °C. Calculate the heat supplied, change in internal energy, and work done by the gas. (Take R = 8.314 J mol^-1 K^-1)
solution_steps: Convert temperatures to Kelvin: T_1 = 27 + 273 = 300 K, T_2 = 127 + 273 = 400 K. Temperature change dT = 100 K.
Calculate change in internal energy: dU = n C_v dT = 2 \times (3/2 R) \times 100 = 300 R.
Calculate C_p: C_p = C_v + R = 5/2 R.
Calculate heat supplied at constant pressure: dQ = n C_p dT = 2 \times (5/2 R) \times 100 = 500 R.
Apply first law to find work done: dW = dQ - dU = 500 R - 300 R = 200 R.

solved_numericals.question: An ideal gas undergoes a cyclic process 1-2-3-1. From 1 to 2, 300 J of heat is added and 100 J of work is done by the gas. From 2 to 3, the process is adiabatic and 150 J of work is done on the gas. From 3 to 1, the gas is compressed back to state 1 with 50 J of heat rejected to the surroundings. Find the internal energy at state 2 if U_1 = 100 J, and find the work done from 3 to 1.
solution_steps: For path 2->3 (adiabatic): dQ_23 = 0, so dU_23 = -dW_23. Given work done ON the gas is 150 J, so dW_23 = -150 J. Thus, dU_23 = 150 J.
For the complete cycle, total internal energy change is zero: \oint dU = 0.
For path 3->1: dQ_31 = -50 J. Using first law for 3->1: dQ_31 = dU_31 + dW_31 => -50 = (U_1 - U_3) + dW_31.

assumptions_and_limitations: The first law assumes macroscopic equilibrium states where pressure and temperature are well-defined throughout the system.
It does not specify the direction of heat transfer or natural processes (which is the domain of the Second Law of Thermodynamics).

common_misconceptions.wrong: Heat and internal energy are the same thing.
common_misconceptions.correct: Heat is energy in transit across a boundary due to a temperature difference, whereas internal energy is an inherent property contained within the system.
common_misconceptions.why: Heat appears only during a process, whereas internal energy is a state function possessing a definite value at any given equilibrium state.

common_misconceptions.wrong: In an isothermal process, because temperature is constant, no heat is exchanged.
common_misconceptions.correct: Heat is exchanged in an isothermal process (Q = W), but it is entirely converted into or derived from work without changing the internal energy.
common_misconceptions.why: Constant temperature means delta U = 0, but dQ = dU + dW implies dQ = dW when dW is non-zero.

quick_revision: The first law of thermodynamics is simply the law of conservation of energy: dQ = dU + dW.
First Law of Thermodynamics (Differential): dQ = dU + dW
Work Done in a Thermodynamic Process: W = \int P \, dV
